title: 2 Samuel 2:1–7
context: After the lament, David inquires of the LORD whether he should go up into any of the cities of Judah. The LORD tells him to go up, and, when David asks where, answers, “To Hebron.” David goes up with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite, and brings his men and their households to live in the cities of Hebron. The men of Judah come and anoint him king over the house of Judah, and they tell him that the men of Jabesh Gilead were the ones who buried Saul. David sends messengers to bless those men by the LORD for the kindness they have shown to Saul, prays that the LORD will show loving kindness and truth to them, promises to reward that kindness, and urges them to be strong and valiant, for Saul is dead and the house of Judah has anointed David king over them. Both traditions read the unit as David seeking the LORD before he moves, and as Judah’s anointing of him over that house alone, not yet over all Israel. His regard for Saul continues in the blessing of Jabesh Gilead. The scene is to be described as the text gives it, without being turned into a type of later events.

verses.text: After this, David inquired of the LORD, saying, “Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah?” The LORD said to him, “Go up.” David said, “Where shall I go up?” He said, “To Hebron.”
verses.arminianNotes:
After this, David inquired of the LORD, saying, “Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah?” The LORD said to him, “Go up.” David said, “Where shall I go up?” He said, “To Hebron.”

Arminian readers hear a real inquiry and a real answer. David does not simply walk into a vacuum left by Saul; he asks whether to go up, and then where, and he goes only when the LORD has named Hebron.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the first move of the new chapter is an inquiry of the LORD. The answers are short and clear: “Go up.” and “To Hebron.” David’s rise over Judah begins with that word, not with a self-appointed march.

Both traditions take the verse as shared ground: the LORD directs the next step, and Hebron is the place he names.

verses.text: So David went up there with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite.
verses.arminianNotes:
So David went up there with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite. The going up of verse 1 is now carried out, and the household is named as the WEB names them.

Arminian readers hear obedience in a simple journey. He goes up there, to Hebron, and he does not go alone; the two wives already known from his Ziklag years go with him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the verse as the outworking of the LORD’s “Go up.” The names are given without adornment: Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail, remembered as the wife of Nabal the Carmelite.

Both traditions read the verse as the actual ascent, shared narrative ground.

verses.text: David brought up his men who were with him, every man with his household. They lived in the cities of Hebron.
verses.arminianNotes:
David brought up his men who were with him, every man with his household. They lived in the cities of Hebron. The move is not David’s only; the band and their families settle in the towns of that region.

Arminian readers hear a real relocation of a whole company. Every man goes with his household, and they live in the cities of Hebron, a settled presence, not a raid.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same bringing up of the men and their households, and the living in the cities of Hebron. The place the LORD named becomes their dwelling, and the next verse’s anointing will happen there.

Both traditions take the verse as the settlement that prepares Judah’s act, on shared ground.

verses.text: The men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. They told David, “The men of Jabesh Gilead were those who buried Saul.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. They told David, “The men of Jabesh Gilead were those who buried Saul.” The anointing is over Judah, and news of Saul’s burial is brought in the same breath.

Arminian readers hear a public, limited kingship. The men of Judah anoint him over their house, not yet over all Israel. They also tell him of Jabesh Gilead’s kindness to Saul, which David will answer in the next verses.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the anointing as the men of Judah’s act at Hebron, over the house of Judah. David’s earlier anointing by Samuel is not repeated here as a scene; this is Judah’s recognition, and it is still only Judah.

Both traditions read the verse as a descriptive beginning of David’s reign in the south, without forcing a type, and as the notice that leads him to bless Jabesh Gilead.

verses.text: David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh Gilead, and said to them, “Blessed are you by the LORD, that you have shown this kindness to your lord, even to Saul, and have buried him.
verses.arminianNotes:
David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh Gilead, and said to them, “Blessed are you by the LORD, that you have shown this kindness to your lord, even to Saul, and have buried him.” The speech that began here continues through verse 7.

Arminian readers hear a blessing, not a rebuke. He commends their kindness to Saul as to their lord, and he does it in the LORD’s name. Regard for the fallen king continues after the lament.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the blessing is “by the LORD,” and that Saul is still called their lord. David honors the men who buried him; the political setting of a new court does not cancel that honor in the text itself.

Both traditions take the verse as shared ground in kindness toward Saul’s memory, the same regard already shown in chapter 1.

verses.text: Now may the LORD show loving kindness and truth to you. I also will reward you for this kindness, because you have done this thing.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now may the LORD show loving kindness and truth to you. I also will reward you for this kindness, because you have done this thing.” David prays for the LORD’s loving kindness and truth, and he also pledges his own reward.

Arminian readers hear both petition and promise. The LORD is asked to show loving kindness and truth; David also binds himself to reward what they have done. The two are held together, not played off against each other.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the LORD’s loving kindness and truth as the first gift named, and David’s reward as a further, human pledge. The kindness they showed Saul is not left without an answer from the new king in Hebron.

Both traditions read the verse as blessing and commitment, shared ground, without a contrast over whether the message is devotion or diplomacy. The text is both a prayer and a king’s word.

verses.text: Now therefore let your hands be strong, and be valiant; for Saul your lord is dead, and also the house of Judah have anointed me king over them.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now therefore let your hands be strong, and be valiant; for Saul your lord is dead, and also the house of Judah have anointed me king over them.” The speech closes with a call to courage and with the news of Judah’s anointing.

Arminian readers hear a frank word to a town that had been loyal to Saul. He tells them Saul is dead, and that Judah has anointed him; he asks them to be strong and valiant. The invitation is real, and it is not dressed up as something other than a new reign in the south.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same close: hands strong, valiant hearts, Saul dead, and David anointed over Judah. The men of Jabesh Gilead are told the truth of the situation and are treated as people who can still act with courage.

Both traditions take the verse as the end of the blessing, descriptive of David’s opening toward that town, not as a typological scene and not as a fork between the two readings.
